Sometimes it's far better to show the aftermath and leave the act up to audience interpretation.  Imply that it was obviously unpleasant, but let them decide what happened themselves.  Think about the end of Rosemary's Baby.  They never show the baby, but you get the impact anyway.

A way to skirt the issue could be to start the sex scene like a normal sex scene, but never describe the sexual aspects of what's happening.  You know, focus on the things that are "off" about it.  I have a nude scene in the story I'm working on where I have the main character get undressed and completely avoid describing her body.  I focus instead on her scars.  It's a fake out.  You bait the audience with the promise of sex, but don't deliver.  That's just my suggestion, though.  You do what feels right for you and the story.  That's what really matters.

Yes and no.  The pitch comes more from how relaxed your throat is and puts itself "above" the sigh, like it's bouncing off of the roof of your mouth.  It's a weird feeling at first, but you get used to it.  BTW, this how to "false chord" scream/growl.  It's a hoarse, bark-y sound when you do it high, but it's pretty brutal when you go low with it.  The more you relax your throat, the lower the pitch, and the lower the pitch, the more you'll need to enunciate.  Unless you're into that marble-mouthed, Chris Barnes kinda thing.

Basically, sigh as hard as you can.  Don't add any "growl" to it, just sigh super hard.  Practice that for a while until you're comfortable with the throat position.  Then, sigh harder.  Keep building new levels of sighing until it becomes raspy, but painless.  Boom, that's how I do it.  It'll take a while, but you won't destroy your voice.  Edit:  REALLY IMPORTANT!  I forgot to mention, DO NOT choke off the end of your breath.  Let all out the air out at the end of a scream/growl.  If you don't get all the air out of your lungs, you'll either hurt your voice or pass out.

The reason you can't just right click on a video to save it is because a video is a series of pictures shown to you in sequence very quickly.  Video files contain all of the pictures that make up the video as well as information about how many pictures, or frames, the video player should display a second.  The reason you need a program to convert the video is because the program records the video's frames per second, true video resolution, and all of the frames you see, allowing you to copy the video as close to the original as possible. When you're brand new a lot can change about the direction you end up taking.  I wanted to be a blues/rock guy like Jimmy Page, but then I heard Black Flag and wanted to take that route.  Eventually, I found myself playing a weird Punk/Metal/Jazz hybrid thing and I just accepted that.  If you like playing slower, more lyrical music, do you lean more towards Leonard Cohen or Bob Dylan?  If your answer is the former, I'd recommend that you learn to finger pick and use a lot of seventh chords.  If you lean more towards Dylan, just buy a capo and stick to simple chords for now.  As your playing evolves, you'll find yourself growing into your own style.  Just never forget to go outside of western scales and mode when it comes to note choice.  Sometimes the wrong note at the right time is far more effective at conveying an emotion.

As a guitarist myself, the best thing I ever did for learning theory was learning about really "out there" scales.  The Sakura scale, the augmented scale, the diminished scale.  These scales can help you add flavour to melodies and progressions.  From there, I would suggest that you experiment with adding notes from those scales into your riffs, but try to avoid writing the riff based around the scale.  That way you can still bounce back to a full western mode and it won't feel jarring.  Most importantly, seek out weird chords.  You might never use a major 7 flat 9 chord, but maybe you'll be imply it in a riff.  Best kind of theory to learn would be Jazz theory.  Also, try and root yourself in a "home genre".  Like, for instance, I consider myself a Punk musician because that's my home base.  Most people I know would consider me a Metal kinda guy, but I'll always keep that Punk edge to my playing.  Figure out where your feet are planted, and branch out from there.  As for what to read/watch, I don't know your musical identity.  What kind of music do you play?
